Compose runs composition, layout and drawing as three separate phases, and zero recompositions means the cost has moved into the other two — so attribute the frame to a phase before you change any code.

### What each phase does and what invalidates it
- **Composition** runs your `@Composable` functions and updates the layout node tree. Invalidated by a snapshot read in a composable body.
- **Layout** measures each child exactly once, then places it. Invalidated by a read inside a measure or placement lambda (`Modifier.offset { }`, a custom `Modifier.layout`), or by a size change.
- **Draw** records draw commands into the render node. Invalidated by a read inside `drawBehind { }`, `drawWithCache { }` or `graphicsLayer { }`.

Invalidation flows forwards only: a recomposition forces layout and draw, but a draw-phase change re-records one layer and touches nothing above it.

### Attributing a slow frame
- The Layout Inspector's recomposition counts answer exactly one question — "is this composition?" — and nothing else.
- A system trace is the real tool. Under `Choreographer#doFrame` the Compose work splits into slices named `Compose:recompose`, `AndroidOwner:measureAndLayout` and `AndroidOwner:draw`; whichever owns the milliseconds names the phase.
- Turn on composition tracing (`androidx.tracing:tracing-perfetto` plus the binary artifact) and the recompose slice breaks down into individual composables by name.
- Read the Frame Timeline track, not the average: fix the frames that actually missed the deadline.

Zero recompositions on a janky frame is good news about your state handling and a pointer at layout or draw — usually deep nesting, a `SubcomposeLayout`, or a shadow, blur or large text layout redrawn every frame.

Stability is a promise about comparison: a type is stable when `equals` is a trustworthy answer to "did this change", and when any change to a public property is published to the composition through snapshot state.

### What the compiler infers on its own
- Primitives, `String`, enums and function types are stable.
- A class is inferred stable when every public property is a `val` of a stable type and it carries no mutable state the runtime cannot observe. A single public `var` of a plain type makes it unstable.
- A type compiled without the Compose compiler plugin — a pure-Kotlin module, a Java library, a generated DTO — gets no inference at all and is therefore treated as unstable.
- Generics carry conditional stability: `data class Page<T>(val items: T)` is stable only for the type arguments that are.

### Why `List<Tag>` is unstable
`List` is a read-only interface, not an immutable type. The object behind it may be an `ArrayList` that someone mutates in place, so `equals` can return true after the contents changed. `kotlinx.collections.immutable`'s `ImmutableList` and `PersistentList` are known to the compiler as stable, so `toImmutableList()` in the ViewModel fixes it at the source.

Since strong skipping this no longer blocks skipping — an unstable parameter is compared by instance identity — but identity is a harsher test than `equals`, so a freshly built but equal list still recomposes the card.

### What the annotations add
- `@Immutable` — every public property is fixed at construction. The strongest claim, and the one to use on UI models.
- `@Stable` — properties may change, but only through snapshot state, and `equals` stays consistent for the life of the instance.
- Neither is verified by anything. Annotate a type that really does mutate silently and you get a screen that never updates — a far worse bug than a wasted recomposition.

Strong skipping makes every restartable composable skippable by comparing unstable parameters with instance identity instead of refusing to skip at all, and it memoizes lambdas for you.

### What changed
- Before, one unstable parameter made a composable non-skippable, so it re-ran whenever its parent ran. Now it is `restartable skippable` in the report regardless.
- Stable parameters are still compared with `equals`; unstable ones with `===`.
- Lambdas declared inside composables are memoized automatically, so the `remember { { ... } }` wrapper that older articles insist on is noise for a plain callback.
- Opt a single function out with `@NonSkippableComposable`, or turn the mode off for the module with `featureFlags.add(ComposeFeatureFlag.StrongSkipping.disabled())` in the `composeCompiler` block.

### What it does not rescue
- **A new instance every recomposition.** `ArticleCard(tags = article.tags.map(::toTag))` builds a fresh list each time, identity never matches, and the card recomposes forever. Move the mapping out of composition.
- **A state read too high in the tree.** Skipping cannot save a composable that its own read invalidates.
- **Non-restartable composables.** Inline lambdas (`Column`, `Row`, `Box` content) and composables that return a value have no restart scope, so there is no place to skip.
- **Expensive bodies.** Formatting a date, sorting a list or decoding an image still costs what it costs on the runs that do happen.
- **Layout and draw.** Skipping is a composition-phase optimisation and does nothing for a slow measure or an overdrawn frame.

The mental model: skipping decides *whether* a function re-runs. Most of the milliseconds people are chasing come from what it does when it does run, and from the two phases after it.

The lambda overload moves the state read out of composition and into the layout phase, so a value changing every frame re-runs placement instead of re-running your composable functions.

### Where each version reads the value
- `Modifier.offset(y = scroll.value.dp)` — the read happens while the composable body runs, in composition. Every frame costs composition, layout and draw for that whole subtree.
- `Modifier.offset { IntOffset(0, scroll.value) }` — the lambda runs during placement. Composition is skipped and measurement is not repeated; only placement and draw run.
- `Modifier.graphicsLayer { translationY = scroll.value.toFloat() }` — the block runs in the draw phase, so only the layer is re-recorded. The cheapest option, and the right one for translation, scale, rotation and alpha.
- The same trick everywhere: `drawBehind { drawRect(color) }` instead of `background(color)`, `graphicsLayer { alpha = x }` instead of `Modifier.alpha(x)`, and a `() -> String` parameter instead of a `String` for a fast-changing label.

### The traps
- The read must be **inside** the lambda. Hoisting it to `val y = scroll.value` above the modifier puts the read back in composition and buys nothing.
- Deferring changes when the value is read, not what layout does with it. `offset` never affects measured size in either form, so siblings do not move and the content can spill outside the parent unless you clip.
- A `graphicsLayer` is a real render node, not free. Setting `compositingStrategy = CompositingStrategy.Offscreen` forces an offscreen buffer, which is exactly the GPU cost you were trying to avoid.

Rule of thumb: ask which phase actually needs the new value, and read it in the latest phase you can get away with.

The reviewer is right: `derivedStateOf` only tracks snapshot state reads, so over ordinary parameters it captures the first values in its closure and never recomputes.

### The three tools and the shape of problem each solves
- **Compute in the body.** Correct whenever the work is cheap and depends on parameters — it re-runs with the composable, which is exactly what you want. A string concat, a `size` check or a boolean does not need caching.
- **`remember(key1, key2) { ... }`.** An expensive pure computation over parameters: filtering, sorting, parsing, building a formatter. It recomputes when a key changes, which for `items` and `query` is precisely the trigger you want.
- **`remember { derivedStateOf { ... } }`.** Reading snapshot state that changes far more often than the answer does. It records what it read, recomputes lazily, and notifies its readers only when the result compares different. `scrollState.firstVisibleItemIndex > 0` is the archetype — the input moves every frame, the boolean flips once.

### What the wrong choice costs
- `derivedStateOf` over parameters is stale forever, because a parameter is not observable. If you need both, key it: `remember(query) { derivedStateOf { ... } }`.
- `derivedStateOf` on a one-to-one mapping adds a snapshot object and a dependency record to produce a value that changes exactly as often as its input.
- `remember` with a missing key is the classic "why is my list not updating" bug — and the one the compiler cannot catch for you.
- No caching at all around real work means it runs on every keystroke.

Ask what makes the value change: parameters → key a `remember`; snapshot state that moves more often than the result → `derivedStateOf`; cheap → just write the expression.

`key` controls identity; `contentType` controls reuse — without it every row is a candidate for every recycled slot, so a slot that held a text row gets handed to a photo row and the runtime throws the whole subtree away instead of updating it.

### What to give the list
- `items(posts, key = { it.id }, contentType = { it.kind })` on every call. The key keeps state and item animations attached to the right row; the content type groups rows whose composition can actually be reused.
- Prefer the `items` / `itemsIndexed` overloads over a `repeat` inside a single `item { }`. One `item` is one slot: the whole block composes at once and nothing is virtualised.
- Keep the row body cheap. No `BoxWithConstraints` (it is a `SubcomposeLayout`, so it composes its content during measurement), no image decode on the main thread, no `SimpleDateFormat` per row — hoist formatting into the model.
- `Modifier.animateItem()`, which replaced `animateItemPlacement()` in Foundation 1.7, needs the key and costs an animation per visible item. Add it where it reads, not everywhere.

### Nesting and measurement
- A `LazyColumn` inside a `Column(Modifier.verticalScroll())` is given an unbounded height constraint and throws. Giving it a fixed height silences the crash and destroys virtualisation — every row composes at once.
- The right shape is one lazy list per scroll axis: turn the surrounding content into `item { }` and `items()` calls in the same `LazyColumn`, with `stickyHeader` where you need one.
- A `LazyRow` inside a `LazyColumn` item is fine — different axis — but give the inner list its own keys, and hoist its `LazyListState` if the horizontal position must survive scrolling away.

Rule of thumb: one lazy list per axis, a `key` and a `contentType` on every `items` call, and nothing in a row body you would be unhappy to run sixty times a second.

Switch on the compiler's reports and metrics in the `composeCompiler` block, build the variant you ship, and read `<module>-composables.txt`, which prints every composable with a `restartable`/`skippable` header and each parameter marked `stable` or `unstable`.

### Turning them on
- The Compose compiler ships inside Kotlin since 2.0 as `org.jetbrains.kotlin.plugin.compose`, so it is configured through the `composeCompiler { }` Gradle extension — `reportsDestination` and `metricsDestination` — not the old `kotlinCompilerExtensionVersion`.
- Output is written per module and per variant at compile time. Gate it behind a Gradle property so ordinary builds and CI do not pay for it, and always read the variant you actually ship.

### What the four files say
- `<module>-composables.txt` — the human-readable one: `restartable skippable fun PostRow(stable post: Post, unstable tags: List<Tag>)`. The parameter marked `unstable` is the answer you came for.
- `<module>-classes.txt` — `stable class` / `unstable class` per type, with the offending field named. This is where you learn that one `var` or one `List` poisoned a whole model.
- `<module>-module.json` — aggregate counts, including `skippableComposables` out of `restartableComposables`. Track the ratio between releases; a drop is a regression.
- `<module>-composables.csv` — the same rows, for scripting a diff.

### What the report cannot tell you
- It is static analysis. It says a function *can* skip, never how often it did — a `skippable` composable still re-runs when a parameter's identity changes every frame, so pair it with recomposition counts.
- Anything from a module compiled without the plugin is reported unstable. That is a build-setup fact, not a modelling mistake.
- Inline composables such as `Column` and `Row` never appear; they have no restart scope of their own.

A recomposition count is how many times that restart scope actually re-ran, and 300 on a static header means something invalidated it 300 times — the Skips column beside it tells you whether the runtime managed to bail out or not.

### Reading the two columns
- **Recompositions** — the scope re-ran its body. **Skips** — it was invalidated, the runtime compared parameters and skipped the body. Many skips and few recompositions is the healthy shape; the number to be alarmed by is recompositions climbing on a composable whose inputs did not change.
- Counts attach to restartable scopes only. `Column`, `Row` and other inline composables have none, so their work shows up on the nearest restartable ancestor.
- Reset the counters, perform exactly one interaction, then read the delta. The total since launch tells you nothing.
- It requires a debuggable build with source information, so trust the counts and ignore the timings from that build.

### Getting from the count to the cause
1. Walk up the tree. If the parent's count matches the header's, the invalidation comes from above and the parent is the composable that could not skip.
2. If the count is the header's own, it reads snapshot state directly — a `collectAsStateWithLifecycle`, a scroll position, an animation value read in the body.
3. Check the compiler report for that function: `restartable` without `skippable`, or a parameter marked `unstable` that is a new instance each frame, explains most cases.
4. Fix by pushing the read down into the leaf that needs it, deferring it into a lambda, or hoisting the allocation out of composition — then reset and measure again.

The counts are a compass, not a verdict: a high count on a trivial composable costs nothing measurable, and a janky frame with zero recompositions means the problem is in layout or draw.

Strong skipping does memoize the lambda, but the memo is keyed on what the lambda captures — capture a value that changes every frame and you allocate a new lambda every frame, so the child's parameter comparison fails.

### Why the memoization does not save you
- The compiler rewrites `{ onSeek(progress) }` into roughly `remember(progress) { { onSeek(progress) } }`. New `progress`, new instance, new parameter value, no skip.
- Wrapping it yourself in `remember { }` with no keys fixes the identity and breaks the callback: it closes over the first `progress` forever and the button seeks to a position from ten seconds ago.
- Strong skipping (default since the Compose compiler shipped with Kotlin 2.0.20) refuses to memoize a lambda that captures an **unstable** value at all — that one is a fresh instance on every recomposition regardless.

### The fix
- `rememberUpdatedState(progress)` keeps one `State` object alive for the whole call site and writes the newest value into it on each composition. The lambda captures the `State`, whose identity never changes, and reads `.value` at the moment it runs.
- Read `.value` inside the lambda body, never in the composable body — a read in the body subscribes the composition to it again and you are back where you started.
- For plain events, pass something whose identity is already stable: a method reference on a `ViewModel` or a `@Stable` state holder, rather than a fresh lambda built over changing data.

### The same shape elsewhere
`LaunchedEffect(Unit)` plus `rememberUpdatedState` is the canonical pair: the effect must not restart when the callback changes, but it must call the newest one.

Rule of thumb: a callback should capture identities, not values. If it needs a number that moves every frame, it should read that number when it fires.

State in Compose is identified by position in the composition, so calling the same composable from a different call site creates a different group: the old one is disposed and a new one built from scratch — `movableContentOf` is the API that relocates a group instead.

### Why position is identity
- The slot table keys every group by its call site, plus whatever `key()` you supplied. `if (wide) Row { Player() } else Column { Player() }` is two call sites; leaving one disposes its `remember`s, cancels its `LaunchedEffect`s and destroys its `LayoutNode`s.
- `rememberSaveable` rescues plain values, not a running effect, an `ExoPlayer` instance, a scroll position object or an animation in flight.

### What `movableContentOf` does
- `remember { movableContentOf { ... } }` wraps the content in a callable whose group the runtime is allowed to move. When it disappears from one call site and reappears at another **within the same composition pass**, the existing slots and nodes are moved over — state, effects and node identity all survive.
- Remove it in one pass and add it in the next and there is nothing left to move: the group has already been discarded and you get a fresh one.
- Invoking the same movable content from two places at once gives two independent copies, not one shared instance.
- Use the parameterised overloads (`movableContentOf<T>`) instead of capturing arguments, or a keyless `remember` freezes them.

### `key()` is the sibling-level version
`key(id) { Row(...) }` fixes identity among siblings of one parent, so a reorder or an insertion keeps each child's state — that is exactly what `LazyColumn`'s `key = { it.id }` does. It cannot move anything between parents.

Rule of thumb: `key` for reordering inside one parent, `movableContentOf` for a subtree that changes parents, `LookaheadScope` on top when you want that move animated rather than instant.

A `composed { }` modifier is a composable that runs once per usage site on every composition, and because two `composed` instances never compare equal it also defeats the equality check the modifier chain would otherwise use to skip work.

### What `composed` costs
- The factory is materialized during composition, so each usage becomes a composition group with its own slots — one per element, per call site, per recomposition. A hundred rows means a hundred little compositions.
- The resulting modifier has no meaningful `equals`, so it cannot be hoisted into a top-level `val` and reused, and a parent that would have skipped now sees a changed `modifier` parameter.
- Every state read inside it invalidates composition, even when only the drawing had to change. An animation written this way recomposes the whole subtree at 60 Hz.

### What a node gives you instead
- You split it in two: a `ModifierNodeElement<T>` data class holding the parameters, with `equals`/`hashCode` for free, and a `Modifier.Node` holding the behaviour and its mutable state.
- On recomposition the runtime diffs elements. Equal means nothing happens at all; different means `update(node)` mutates the existing node — no allocation, no group, no composition.
- The node implements only the interfaces it needs — `DrawModifierNode`, `LayoutModifierNode`, `PointerInputModifierNode`, `SemanticsModifierNode` — and invalidates exactly one phase with `invalidateDraw()`, `invalidateMeasurement()` or `invalidatePlacement()`.
- It has a real lifecycle (`onAttach`/`onDetach`) and its own `coroutineScope`, so an animation can run entirely inside the node and never touch the composition. `currentValueOf(LocalContentColor)` reads a CompositionLocal without subscribing a composable to it.

`composed` still exists but the framework has moved all of its own modifiers off it. The mental model: `composed` puts your modifier in the composition, a node puts it in the layout tree — anything that reacts per frame belongs in the tree, where invalidating draw alone is possible.

`BoxWithConstraints` is a `SubcomposeLayout`: it moves the composition of its children into the measure pass, so each row now composes during layout, every time it is measured, instead of once during composition.

### What subcomposition costs
- The content cannot be composed until constraints exist, so the runtime runs a nested composition inside the layout phase. That work is not batched with normal composition and is not skipped by the usual parameter comparison.
- Each `SubcomposeLayout` carries its own `SubcomposeLayoutState` with slot bookkeeping and a reuse policy. A hundred of them in a scrolling list is a hundred separate little compositions being created and thrown away.
- Intrinsics are the worst case: a parent asking for `minIntrinsicHeight` forces the subcomposition to run again, because there is no way to answer without composing first.
- A state read inside the block invalidates layout *and* the subcomposition, so a size-driven animation recomposes on every frame.

### What to use instead
- If constraints only change how you **measure**, not **what** you compose, use `Modifier.layout { measurable, constraints -> }` or a custom `Layout`. No subcomposition at all.
- If a parent must size itself to its largest child, `IntrinsicSize.Min` / `Max` costs one extra measure pass and zero extra composition.
- If the final size drives an animation or a placement, `LookaheadScope` gives you the target size without recomposing on it.
- Read the breakpoint once, high up — one `BoxWithConstraints` around the whole list, or `currentWindowAdaptiveInfo()` — and pass a boolean down.

### The trap underneath
`Measurable.measure()` may be called only once per child per layout pass; a second call throws. That restriction is exactly why people reach for `SubcomposeLayout` when what they actually wanted was intrinsics.

`LazyLayout` is subcomposition used correctly: compose only what is visible and reuse the slots — which is also why `contentType` matters, since a slot is only reusable for the same content type. Reach for `SubcomposeLayout` when the content itself depends on the constraints; if only the numbers do, it is a `Layout`.

Three real options — declare the class stable in a stability configuration file, map it into a type you own, or apply the Compose compiler to the module that produces it — and only the middle one is a promise you can actually keep.

### Why it is unstable in the first place
- The compiler infers stability from a class's fields, but across a module boundary it can only do that from metadata the Compose compiler plugin writes. A class from a plain Kotlin or Java artifact carries none, so it is unstable even if every field is a `val`.
- `List`, `Map` and `Set` are interfaces that could be backed by a mutable implementation, so a single `List<Post>` field makes the whole class unstable too.

### The three options
- **Stability configuration file** — `composeCompiler { stabilityConfigurationFiles.add(...) }`, one fully-qualified name per line, `*` wildcards allowed. Zero code. It is an unchecked promise: name a class that really does mutate in place and Compose skips a recomposition that was needed, and you debug stale UI rather than a crash.
- **A UI model you own** — map the SDK type at the ViewModel boundary into your own `data class` with `ImmutableList` fields from `kotlinx.collections.immutable`. Costs mapping code, buys a UI layer that does not break when their schema changes. This is the answer for anything you did not write.
- **Apply the Compose compiler plugin to the module** — works when the offending module is yours; the plugin emits the metadata and stability is inferred, no annotations required.

### What strong skipping changed about the answer
Unstable parameters no longer block skipping at all — they are compared by instance identity instead of `equals`. So an unstable type only hurts when the producer hands out a new instance on every emission. Check that first: a repository that re-emits the same cached object skips perfectly well while unstable.

Annotate what you can prove, wrap what you cannot.

Everything on that first pass is cold: ART is interpreting code that has never been compiled, classes are still being loaded, the slot table and layout tree are being built for the first time, and the glyph and shader caches are empty.

### What is cold, in order
1. **Code.** A fresh install has no AOT-compiled profile, so the Compose runtime, the layout system and your composables all run interpreted until JIT catches up. Compose puts far more framework code on the critical path than the View system, which is why the effect is more visible here.
2. **Classes.** Every composable lambda is a class. A single screen loads thousands, and loading plus verification happens on the thread producing the frame.
3. **Composition.** The first pass allocates every slot-table group and every `LayoutNode`; later passes only diff. Inside a `LazyColumn`, each distinct item layout pays this again the first time it scrolls into view.
4. **Draw.** RenderThread compiles the shader programs for effects it has not drawn before, and the text stack rasterises each glyph into the atlas once per typeface and size.

### What fixes which part
- A **baseline profile** fixes point 1, and it covers `androidx.compose.*` as well as your own code because those classes ship inside your APK — which is why Compose apps gain more from one than View apps do. Generate it with the `androidx.baselineprofile` plugin and a `BaselineProfileRule` test that drives *this* journey: launch, open the screen, fling the list.
- Points 2 to 4 get nothing from AOT. Fewer distinct item layouts, honest `contentType` values and prefetching a couple of rows off-screen are what cut them.
- Verify rather than assume: run the scroll with `CompilationMode.None()` and again with `CompilationMode.Partial()` and compare `FrameTimingMetric`.

The quick tell that you are looking at a first-run problem and not at your own code: `adb shell cmd package compile -f -m speed <pkg>` compiles everything ahead of time, and if the jank vanishes it was never your composables.

Use two gates with different characters: a compiler-metrics diff that is fully deterministic and runs in seconds on every PR, and a Macrobenchmark scroll on one fixed device that only means anything once you control the noise.

### The cheap deterministic gate
- Turn on `composeCompiler { metricsDestination = ... }` and commit the generated `*-module.json` per module. It records `skippableComposables`, `restartableComposables` and the counts of stable and unstable parameters — pure compiler output, byte-identical for identical sources.
- CI rebuilds it and diffs against the committed copy. A composable that stopped being skippable, or a newly unstable parameter type, fails the PR with a one-line reason. No device, no flake, no minutes.
- Its blind spot: it says nothing about runtime behaviour. A perfectly skippable composable that gets invalidated on every frame still passes.

### The scroll gate
- Macrobenchmark with `FrameTimingMetric`, a scripted fling over fixed seeded data — no network, no live clock, no variable-length animation. Report `frameDurationCpuMs` and `frameOverrunMs` at P50/P90/P99; the tail is where jank lives, the median hides it.
- Pin what dominates the number: one device model and OS image, locked clocks, `CompilationMode.Partial()` because that is what a real install runs, at least 10 iterations, the first discarded as warmup.
- Compare the PR against its merge base **in the same job on the same device**, not against a figure recorded last week. Thermal state and an OS update move the absolute number far more than most regressions do.
- Gate on a relative threshold with slack in it, around 10-15% on P90, and run it on the merge queue or behind a label, because a device job costs minutes.

The failure mode to design against is not a missed regression, it is a flaky gate — one red build nobody can reproduce and the whole thing gets switched off within a month.

Look for offscreen buffers and fill rate: an alpha or a blur that forces the renderer to allocate a layer, shadows and non-rectangular clips, and stacked opaque backgrounds painting the same pixels several times over.

### The usual offenders
- **Alpha.** `Modifier.alpha(0.5f)` is `graphicsLayer { alpha = 0.5f }`, and `CompositingStrategy.Auto` promotes a layer with alpha below 1 into an offscreen buffer so overlapping children do not double-blend. When the children do not overlap, `CompositingStrategy.ModulateAlpha` applies the alpha per draw operation and skips the buffer entirely.
- **Shadows and clipping.** `Modifier.shadow(elevation, shape, clip = true)` and `Surface(shadowElevation = ...)` draw from an outline. A rounded rectangle has a fast path; an arbitrary `GenericShape` becomes a path clip plus its own layer, on every row of the list.
- **Blur.** `Modifier.blur()` is a `RenderEffect` — API 31 and up, a no-op below — and it re-renders its subtree into a buffer on every frame its content changes.
- **Overdraw.** A `Surface` inside a `Surface` inside a `Box(Modifier.background(...))` paints the same pixels three times. Across a full-screen list that is pure fill rate.
- **Blamed on the GPU but not GPU work:** `painterResource` decodes on the calling thread during composition, and a bitmap decoded at full resolution for a thumbnail costs memory and fill both.

### Measuring instead of guessing
- Developer options, **Debug GPU overdraw**, colours each pixel by how many times it was painted. Blue is fine, red is a bug you can see without a profiler.
- A Perfetto system trace puts RenderThread next to the frame timeline: long `DrawFrame` slices while the UI thread sits idle means the problem is draw, not recomposition.
- `adb shell dumpsys gfxinfo <pkg> framestats` gives the per-frame breakdown, and `FrameTimingMetric` turns the same data into a number you can track over time.

The mental model: composition decides what to draw, but the renderer pays for how many layers and how many times over. Every offscreen buffer is a texture allocated, drawn into, then drawn again.
